Hefei University of Technology, China
Abstract—Prefix caching introduces a fundamental tradeoff in
multi-agent large language model (LLM) serving: retaining a long
system-prompt key–value (KV) cache for an agent accelerates
future calls, yet it reduces the GPU memory available for
batching concurrent requests. In multi-stage workflows, existing
schedulers tend to prioritize either immediate prefix locality or
overall workflow progress. However, under a shared KV cache
budget, optimizing either objective in isolation can prolong task-
level job completion time (JCT) through downstream delays
or frequent prefix replacement. To strike a balance, we here
propose TOPAS, a Task-Oriented Prefix-Aware Scheduler that
jointly decides which agent prefixes to keep in the cache and
which requests to schedule for execution. TOPAS scores candidate
post-decision states by trading off the expected reduction in
each task’s longest remaining service path against the near-term
benefit of downstream prefix reuse, accounting for the costs of
prefix movement and preemption. A task-level aging mechanism
is also incorporated to prevent starvation. We implement TOPAS
within the SGLang framework and assess its performance on
three synthetic DAGs and two MetaGPT software-development
workflows. Compared with the best-performing baseline for each
workload and metric, TOPAS reduces the mean/p99 JCT by
up to 39.8%/49.4% on the synthetic workloads, while lowering
mean JCT by 9.8% on MetaGPT-SOP and mean/p99 JCT by
22.0%/26.6% on MetaGPT-TL.
I. INTRODUCTION
Multi-agent LLM applications tackle complex tasks
via interdependent requests generated by role-specialized
agents [20], [32]. Each request contains an agent-specific
static prefix whose KV cache is reusable across requests from
the same agent in different tasks. Serving systems such as
SGLang maintain cached KV pairs in a radix tree, where
requests sharing the same agent prefix traverse the static path
and each appends its own request-specific dynamic content.
Retaining this cache in GPU memory—referred to as prefix
residency—eliminates redundant prefill computations, yet it
contends with concurrently executing requests for the limited
KV budget. Long system prompts further amplify both the
reuse benefit and the residency cost. Consequently, request
scheduling influences not only task progress but also the
overall serving capacity of the GPU.
Mainstream inference frameworks such as SGLang focus
on optimizing batching, prefix caching, and KV cache man-
agement [11], [37]. Their schedulers primarily operate at
the request level, ranking ready requests using engine-local
information. Although well suited for per-request execution
optimization, this request-level view offers only an indirect
reflection of the inter-request dependencies and program-level
progress that the orchestration layer monitors.
Recent efforts aim to bridge this abstraction gap through
distinct strategies. Parrot and Autellix incorporate application
dataflow or program-level progress into request scheduling
[13], [16], whereas KVFlow leverages workflow context for
prefix-cache placement [18]. These systems primarily optimize
application progress, cache availability, or resource placement,
while prefix residency remains largely separate from request
admission. This decoupling can leave heterogeneous prefixes
co-residing in the cache—reducing the feasible concurrent
batch size—or provoke repeated prefix evictions and reloads
as execution shifts across agents.
An inherent conflict exists between end-to-end progress
against prefix reuse. Consolidating requests from the same
agent allows fewer resident prefixes to support a larger batch,
yet it can stall upstream execution while downstream tasks
remain pending. Conversely, prioritizing workflow progress
tends to trigger frequent agent switching, sacrificing reuse
and incurring significant prefix-movement overhead. Conse-
quently, a scheduler must reconcile prefix locality with holistic
progress, rather than optimizing either objective in isolation.
We therefore pose the following question: How can a
serving system coordinate prefix residency and request
admission throughout workflow execution to minimize
task-level job completion time (JCT) under a constrained
GPU-memory budget? We formalize this problem as online
prefix-state scheduling. At each scheduling point, the scheduler
jointly decides which agent prefixes to retain and which ready
requests to admit, subject to a shared KV cache budget. This
joint decision determines the current batch capacity, immediate
task progress, and the set of prefixes most likely to be reused
by subsequent workflow steps.
To solve this problem, we propose TOPAS, a Task-Oriented
Prefix-Aware Scheduler whose key novelty lies in treating pre-
fix residency as an explicit workflow-level scheduling decision,
jointly optimized with request admission, rather than as an
indirect byproduct of request ordering and cache eviction. To
our knowledge, TOPAS is the first multi-agent LLM scheduler
to jointly optimize prefix residency and request admission for
task-level JCT under a shared KV budget. TOPAS conducts a
hierarchical search to construct post-decision GPU states, each
specifying a resident-prefix set and a compatible allocation
of admitted requests. It selects the optimal state via a JCT-
arXiv:2608.25523v1 [cs.CL] 26 Aug 2026</page><page num="2">oriented utility that trades off anticipated reduction in each
task’s longest remaining service path and near-term prefix
reuse, accounting for the costs of prefix movement and pre-
emption. Our contributions are summarized as:
• We formalize the online prefix-state scheduling problem,
which jointly selects resident agent prefixes and admitted
requests under a shared KV cache budget. Our diagnostic
analysis reveals that heterogeneous prefix co-residency
reduces dynamic batch capacity, while locality-first and
progress-first policies fail in complementary leading to
bad performance.
• We introduce TOPAS, an online scheduler that jointly
determines prefix residency and request admission via
a JCT-oriented utility function. This utility balances
expected reductions in tasks’ longest remaining service
paths and near-term prefix reuse. A task-level aging
mechanism is also incorporated to prevent starvation.
• We implement TOPAS atop SGLang and evaluate it
on three synthetic DAG workloads and two MetaGPT
workloads. Compared with the best-performing baseline
per workload and metric, TOPAS reduces mean/p99 JCT
by up to 39.8%/49.4% on the synthetic workloads; lowers
mean JCT by 9.8% on MetaGPT-SOP; and achieves
mean and p99 JCT reductions by 22.0% and 26.6%,
respectively, on MetaGPT-TL.
II. MOTIVATION: A PROGRESS–REUSE CONFLICT
Task-level policies can use workflow dependencies to decide
which tasks or stages should advance, but their decisions are
ultimately executed by a request-level serving engine. The
engine repeatedly admits ready requests into a continuous
batch under a finite KV budget. Same-agent requests reuse
a resident static-prefix cache, while each request consumes
additional KV capacity for its dynamic suffix and decode to-
kens. Admission order and cache eviction therefore determine
both which prefixes remain resident and how many requests
can run together. Task-level priority alone does not control this
prefix–batch interaction; the following diagnostics isolate its
two consequences.
To examine how request order affects batching, we use
a two-agent microbenchmark on the native LLM serving
runtime. The workload contains n independent requests for
each of agents A and B. The agents have distinct long prefixes,
while all requests use the same dynamic suffix and decode
length. ALTERNATING orders them as A, B, A, B, . . ., keeping
both prefixes resident for most of the run, whereas GROUPED
serves each agent’s requests together. Both orders contain the
same requests and use the same KV budget; only their order
differs.
Table I shows that GROUPED doubles the average running
batch size; ALTERNATING takes 1.8–1.9× as long to finish
the workload. Serving same-agent requests together lets one
resident prefix support a larger batch. Alternating between
agents instead divides KV capacity across both long prefixes,
leaving less space for dynamic suffixes and decode tokens.

The batching benefit in Diagnostic 1 suggests a natural re-
sponse: favor requests that can reuse a resident prefix. Longest
Prefix Match (LPM) is a representative locality-first policy:
it prioritizes ready requests with the longest immediately
reusable prefix. Yet it does not actively choose a target prefix
state. It operates in a reactive, arrival-driven manner: request
order and cache eviction determine prefix residency, which
then becomes the locality signal for the next decision. In an
A → B → C workflow with continuous arrivals at A, this
feedback keeps service near the workflow entrance and delays
stages B and C. To test whether active control can break
this behavior, we augment LPM with a simple downstream
gate that prioritizes C once its backlog accumulates. Figure 1
shows that this coarse intervention achieves lower mean JCT
than LPM.
Progress-first scheduling lies at the other extreme. Shortest
Remaining Processing Time (SRPT) prioritizes tasks with
shorter remaining processing time and can move them toward
the workflow exit. Yet it has no explicit notion of prefix
residency: repeatedly following the shortest remaining work
switches between agents, causing prefix transfers or recompu-
tation and reducing effective service capacity. At the same
operating point, the downstream-gated policy also achieves
lower mean JCT than SRPT. Thus, neither immediate prefix
locality nor task progress alone is sufficient to minimize task-
level JCT.

The two diagnostics in Section II point to a limitation of
request-level scheduling. When requests are chosen one at a
time, prefix residency is determined indirectly by request order
and the serving runtime’s cache-eviction policy. Different

# Paper Summary: EU AI Act in Agile Software Development

**Full Abstract:**
"The EU AI Act requires providers and deployers of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems to implement documentation, risk management, and human oversight. Agile teams that ship AI features in short iterations lack specific artifacts to discharge these duties, since the regulation's abstract provisions do not map onto the Definition of Done, Sprint Reviews, or working agreements. We provide agile teams with an actionable compliance instrument: an evaluated guideline that operationalizes EU AI Act obligations as activities integrable into existing agile practice. We further document the translation method behind it so that the approach can be reused for adjacent regulations."

# Paper Summary: AI Bill of Materials Completeness in Hugging Face Models

## Full Abstract
"Pretrained machine learning (ML) models help developers build ML-intensive software systems without training models from scratch. However, model repositories often provide incomplete machine-readable documentation about model provenance, licenses, datasets, limitations, and external references, creating transparency and governance gaps across the AI supply chain. Artificial Intelligence Bills of Materials (AIBOMs) address these gaps by documenting AI artifacts, including models, metadata, licenses, datasets, model-card information, and external references. Taking public Hugging Face (HF) model repositories as a case study, this paper empirically investigates AIBOM completeness, defined as the extent to which repositories provide AIBOM-relevant information for machine-readable AI supply-chain documentation. We examine approximately 97.5K AIBOM artifacts to assess the extent to which generated AIBOMs: (i) contain required structural and metadata fields, (ii) represent model identity, license, and external-reference information, (iii) capture model-card documentation such as datasets, limitations, safety-risk assessment, and environmental information, and (iv) vary in documentation coverage across repository and artifact characteristics such as task, license availability, dataset declaration, model family, and paper reference. Results indicate that generated AIBOMs provide complete coverage of required AIBOM structure but limited AI-specific documentation completeness. Required fields are fully represented, but model-card, metadata, responsible-use, environmental, limitation, and meaningful-description fields remain weakly represented or missing across generated artifacts."

## V1 Submission Date
July 19, 2026

## Authors
- Md Erfan
- Ahmed Ryan
- Md Rayhanur Rahman

**Affiliations:** Not provided in the webpage content

## Concrete Numbers
- **97.5K** AIBOM artifacts examined
- **12** pages (paper length)

# Paper Summary

**Title:** "Trajectories That Segment Themselves: Agent-Declared Boundaries as a Training Unit"

**ArXiv ID:** 2608.02302

**V1 Submission Date:** August 3, 2026

**Author:** Jingxi Wei (affiliation not listed on this page)

## Abstract

The paper addresses misalignment between long-horizon agent trajectories and training units. The authors propose "collection-time semantic self-segmentation," where agents declare their own boundaries during trajectory generation using falsifiable causal hypotheses. Key features include:

- Agents expose variable-length semantic phases without requiring milestone vocabularies or retrospective segmentation
- The protocol generates "wrong-cause-then-correction transitions" rarely found in recorded work, yielding four supervised targets per collection
- Reviewers can negate hypotheses by name, creating audit supervision from failed regions

## Key Results

**Attribution Test:** Models attributed action blocks to governing hypotheses "at over twice chance" compared to equal-length blocks (paired sign test p = 0.0002).

**Boundary Placement:** A code-blind annotator matched 24 of 40 boundaries; random placement matched 11.5.

**Downstream Performance:** DPO training on 2,551 phase-boundary pairs changed no decisions on 91 adversarial held-out items, while four of 60 changed on matched-construction items (all improving).

**Dataset:** 1,825 pairs from one generator were evaluated.

# Paper Summary: "Spurious Advantage Hidden in GRPO"

**Full Abstract:**
"Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is widely studied for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where its advantage estimator assigns each rollout a magnitude from within-group reward statistics. In the common case, this magnitude rewards rollouts that reach the correct answer through reasoning. Yet, an overlooked case shares the same surface: a rollout may land on it by guessing, and the formula still assigns a high magnitude, which we identify as the spurious advantage. This arises in three cases: bounded-answer tasks with a small candidate set; open-answer sets hosting bounded sub-cases; and search agents whose budget opens many paths to the same answer. In all three, this misleads the policy toward guess-like behaviors. We propose SIGNBALANCE, whose magnitude is composition-free: it keeps the verifier sign, uses a global scale, and restores zero-mean balance via a stop-gradient per-class rescaling. Across math and search agent benchmarks at different scales, SIGNBALANCE matches GRPO on open-answer math and improves on bounded-answer math and search agents."

**v1 Submission Date:** September 3, 2026

**Authors:** Jiamian Wang, Samyadeep Basu, Koustava Goswami, Tong Yu, Zhiqiang Tao

**Affiliations:** Not specified in the provided content

**Concrete Numbers Reported:** None explicitly stated in the abstract or metadata provided

# arXiv sweep, 2026-06-01 to 2026-09-07

Scope: arXiv only. Every paper below was opened and read (abstract plus the results table or section that carries the number quoted); the four marked *abstract only* were read on their arXiv abstract page and are flagged in `items.json`. All dates are the arXiv v1 stamp on the PDF unless noted.

The single most important shift in this window: **the harness stopped being infrastructure and became both a trained object and a measured object.** Three separate benchmarks for harness engineering appeared inside five weeks, two labs published harness-native RL frameworks, and one lab trained a model whose job is to emit a harness. Daliesk's goals 1 and 4 are now a contested research area, not a niche.

---

## 1. RL from verifiable rewards, run inside the real harness

The clearest competitive signal is that RL is moving *into* production scaffolds rather than into simplified training loops.

**LEGO-RL** (Huawei + CUHK, [2608.17393](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17393), 2026-08-18) trains a policy inside unmodified OpenHands SDK, Claude Code and OpenCode by intercepting the model-serving boundary with an in-process proxy that captures exact token ids, log-probabilities, response masks and MoE routing decisions, then replays routing at training time. Qwen3.5-35B-A3B under GSPO improves on SWE-bench Verified 64.0→70.4 (OpenHands SDK), 62.4→68.2 (Claude Code), 57.2→66.6 (OpenCode), with rollout–training probability correlation above 0.99. The paper's most useful engineering numbers are the losses: 7.1% of Claude Code, 2.4% of OpenHands and 6.4% of OpenCode trajectories are excluded from optimisation as infrastructure failures, and ~2.5% of inspected candidate tasks carried verifier logic that mis-applies the reference patch. Their task funnel is 36,884 → 22,806 (rules) → 21,681 (build/verifier validation) → 2,699 (kept only tasks solved 1–3 times in 4 trials). Framework, checkpoints and the 2,699-task index are open.

**Train What You Deploy** (KunlunMeta, [2609.04678](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04678), 2026-09-04) makes the same argument more sharply and adds the missing agent-side half: a machine-checked "training mode" in the production agent binary that provably emits **zero background model calls** (a regression test asserts exactly two provider requests across a tool round-trip), plus negotiated per-request headers for sub-agent depth and reasoning replay that **fail closed** when unattributable. Its C-DPPO certification result (+3.0 points on TMax-100 at two scales) sits below its own stated noise floor and the authors say so; the contribution worth stealing is the protocol, not the algorithm.

**CompactionRL** (Tsinghua + Z.ai, [2607.05378](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05378), 2026-07-06) trains compaction itself. Compaction segments and execution segments share one terminal reward under PPO with token-level loss normalisation and a cross-trajectory GAE correction that discounts earlier segments by the token count of everything after them. GLM-4.5-Air (106B-A30B) reaches 66.8% SWE-bench Verified (+7.0) and 24.5% Terminal-Bench 2.0 (+3.1); GLM-4.7-Flash (30B-A3B) +5.5/+6.8. The framing number: holding the execution agent fixed and swapping only the *summariser* moved SWE-bench Verified from 49.0 to 55.5. Now deployed in the GLM-5.2 (750B-A40B) RL pipeline. This is the strongest single argument that Daliesk's `dsh-compaction` seam is a trainable policy, not a utility.

On credit assignment, **CREST** ([2608.13179](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.13179), Zhejiang + Ant Group AWorld, 2026-08-13) formalises the rule Daliesk should adopt: the verifier sets the **sign** of every token's advantage and a privileged self-teacher only modulates the **magnitude**, gated by student entropy, with a proved bias bound of ~8.4%. Turn-segmented advantages plus that gate take BFCL V3 from 22.12 to 52.00 (Qwen3-4B) versus 43.63 for plain GRPO. **SIGNBALANCE** ([2609.04063](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04063), 2026-09-03, *abstract only*) identifies a related failure: GRPO's within-group magnitude rewards rollouts that reached the right answer by guessing, which matters most for bounded-answer tasks and for search agents whose budget opens many paths to one answer.

For the 120B-scale question, **Post-Training Science for SFT** (Baseten, [2609.01244](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01244), 2026-09-01) is the most directly usable calibration paper of the window: the optimal LoRA learning rate is **flat at 1e-3** across 0.6–32B and two families, roughly 33× the full-fine-tuning optimum; LoRA recovers a **median 98%** of full fine-tuning's improvement at 3.1–12.6% of parameters, and the gap narrows with scale (0.008 nats at 0.6B → 0.003 at 32B); rank plateaus at 64 with α=32; **an MoE fine-tunes like a dense model at the geometric mean of its active and total parameters**; validation loss ranks judged quality within a recipe (Spearman −0.38 to −0.88) but not across model families. **Kimi K3** ([2607.24653](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24653), Moonshot, v2 2026-08-07) is the open-weights baseline to measure against: 2.8T total / 104B activated, 1M context, weights released, Terminal-Bench 2.1 88.3 and SWE-Marathon 42.0 — and, crucially for Daliesk, it trains inside a **unified white-box RL environment that treats the harness as configurable composable modules** and randomises across Kimi Code / Claude Code / Codex / OpenClaw / Hermes during RL specifically to avoid overfitting to one tool schema or context-management policy.

## 2. Reward integrity is now quantified, and it is worse than assumed

Four independent measurements converge. **Auditing Reward Hackability** ([2606.16062](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16062), 2026-06-14): 28.5% of a 49-task SWE-bench Verified sample admits a Docker-verified incorrect patch; 25.0% on R2E-Gym at a strictly weaker attack budget; and a random-effects meta-analysis over **134 frontier submissions** finds Pass@1 is **+14.14pp higher on flagged-hackable tasks within the same human-difficulty stratum** (95% CI [+11.80, +16.48], I²=0%, 123/134 positive). Its methodology finding matters more: an LLM judge endorsed 10 of 11 test-hardening repairs, but a Docker gold-sanity gate then flagged **61.9% of LLM-generated blocking tests as failing on the gold patch itself**.

**Hacker–Fixer loops** (CMU + Fewshot, [2606.08960](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08960), 2026-06-08) audit 1,968 tasks across five terminal benchmarks and find **323 (16%) hackable**, 13/89 in Terminal-Bench 2.0, released as *Terminal Wrench* (323 environments, 3,632 hack trajectories). Their loop — hacker, fixer, and a **solver that vetoes over-restrictive patches** — plus a cross-task shared defence pool drives KernelBench attack success from 62%→0% and Terminal Bench unhinted 39.2%→16.7%, but hardened verifiers also reject 11pp more legitimate solutions. **Hack-Verifiable Terminal Bench** ([2608.22103](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.22103), 2026-08-22) plants detectable honeypots so hacks are flagged by `inotify` rather than judged: ablation hack rates of 22.7–47.7% across five frontier agents, still 16.3% for gemini-3.1-pro even when explicitly told not to read `admin/`; hacks concentrate early, half within the first quarter of a trajectory.

**The Verification Horizon** (Qwen Team, [2606.26300](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26300), 2026-06-24) is the framing document: scalability, faithfulness and robustness cannot be had at once, and no fixed reward survives a strengthening policy. Their behaviour monitor — a pattern set refreshed from rollouts each training interval — takes hacked-resolved from 28.57% to 0.56% while raising *clean* resolved from 40.22% to 60.53% across three SWE-bench variants. Without it, verifier pass rate keeps rising while clean performance collapses late in training. **HackProbe** ([2609.04665](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04665), 2026-09-04) attacks the self-improvement variant with a secret distribution-fixed probe core, a calibrated family-wise p-value, and a reselection layer that returns at most log₂Π bits to the host so the monitor never becomes a second score: AUROC 0.763 vs 0.663, FPR 0.706→0.434, and a probe-size budget that grows as 1/δ².

## 3. Harness engineering as a measured capability — the direct threat

**Prime Agent** (Prime Intellect + Princeton + MIT, [2608.23552](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23552), 2026-08-24, open source) is the closest public analogue of Daliesk's goal 1. An L0–L3 state hierarchy (weights / active context / persistent REPL and recursive subagents / disk-backed history, memories, skills, prompts, subagent specs), with compaction rewriting L1, "agentic garbage collection" managing L2, and versioned refinement updating L3. ARC-AGI-3 RHAE rises 30%→95.5%; an 85.5-hour autonomous nanoGPT run produced 19 validated records. Their sharpest measurement is behavioural, not scoreboard: DeepSeek V4 Pro created **7.6 out-of-loop experiments per 100 training runs under Prime Agent versus 1.2 under Claude Code**.

---

## What Daliesk should do

Harness choice moves paired pass rate 0–8pp but tokens per solved task up to 41.9×; a leaderboard that omits cost is not a decision instrument. Adopt tokens-per-solved-task, no-action turns and a failure-category vector as first-class scorekeeper facts.
9. **Size experiments with a variance decomposition before trusting a delta** (goal 4, experiments with paired seeds). 10. **Build the EU AI Act artifacts now, as generated outputs of the composition manifest** (goal 3 + commercial, composition manifest + sign-off records + data-use terms). At ~120B the systemic-risk tier is not the constraint; documentation, the training-data summary and provenance are. Pair the content-addressed component identity already in goal 4 with an AIBOM-shaped release that fills the fields the Hugging Face study found missing — datasets, limitations, responsible use, environmental information — and pin data-use terms to sessions so the training-data summary is a derivation from the ledger rather than a document written afterwards. Use the Zenodo provision dataset to state, per client jurisdiction, which duties actually bind.

# arXiv sweep, 2026-06-01 to 2026-09-07

Scope: arXiv only. Every paper below was opened and read (abstract plus the results table or section carrying the number quoted); the items marked *abstract only* were read on their arXiv abstract page and are flagged in `items.json`. Dates are the arXiv v1 stamp on the PDF unless noted.

The most important shift in this window: **the harness stopped being infrastructure and became both a trained object and a measured object.** Three benchmarks for harness engineering appeared within five weeks, two labs published harness-native RL frameworks, and one lab trained a model whose job is to emit a harness. ---

**LEGO-RL** (Huawei + CUHK, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17393, 2026-08-18) trains a policy inside unmodified OpenHands SDK, Claude Code and OpenCode by intercepting the model-serving boundary with an in-process proxy that captures exact token ids, log-probabilities, response masks and MoE routing decisions, then replays routing at training time. Qwen3.5-35B-A3B under GSPO improves SWE-bench Verified 64.0 to 70.4 (OpenHands SDK), 62.4 to 68.2 (Claude Code), 57.2 to 66.6 (OpenCode), with rollout-training probability correlation above 0.99. The engineering numbers matter more than the scores: 7.1% of Claude Code, 2.4% of OpenHands and 6.4% of OpenCode trajectories are excluded from optimisation as infrastructure failures, and roughly 2.5% of inspected candidate tasks carried verifier logic that mis-applies the reference patch. Their task funnel is 36,884 to 22,806 (rules) to 21,681 (build/verifier validation) to 2,699 (kept only tasks solved 1-3 times in 4 trials). Framework, checkpoints and the 2,699-task index are open.

**Train What You Deploy** (KunlunMeta, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04678, 2026-09-04) makes the same argument and adds the agent-side half: a machine-checked training mode in the production binary that provably emits **zero background model calls** (a regression test asserts exactly two provider requests across a tool round-trip), plus negotiated per-request headers for sub-agent depth and reasoning replay that **fail closed** when a span cannot be attributed. Its C-DPPO result (+3.0 points on TMax-100 at two scales) sits below its own stated noise floor and the authors say so; the contribution worth stealing is the protocol, not the algorithm.

**CompactionRL** (Tsinghua + Z.ai, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05378, 2026-07-06) trains compaction itself. Compaction and execution segments share one terminal reward under PPO with token-level loss normalisation and a cross-trajectory GAE correction that discounts earlier segments by the token count of everything after them. GLM-4.5-Air (106B-A30B) reaches 66.8% SWE-bench Verified (+7.0) and 24.5% Terminal-Bench 2.0 (+3.1); GLM-4.7-Flash (30B-A3B) gains +5.5/+6.8. Re-solving beats imitating the source trajectory by a wide margin (52.1 against 36.7 average). **SETA** (CAMEL-AI et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.10891, 2026-07-12) releases 4,567 verified terminal environments with difficulty-adaptive evolution and a partial-progress reward that lifts the share of reward-varying tasks from 49% to 86%; an 8B model reaches about 11-12% on Terminal-Bench 2.0, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash goes 40 to 43 pass@1.

On measurement: **DeepSWE** (Datacurve, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.07946, 2026-07-08) authors 113 original tasks across 91 repos never merged upstream, graded by hand-written functional verifiers - an independent judge disagrees with its verdicts **1.4% of the time against 32.4% for SWE-Bench Pro's inherited tests**. **SWE-Bench ProMax** (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09802, 2026-08-10) moves to multilingual refactoring (170 instances, 11.4 files / 261.6 LOC average); the best model reaches 41.2%, GLM-5 gets 36.5% at $0.24/instance against Claude Sonnet 4.6's 38.8% at $4.77, and scaffold change alone moves GPT-5.2 from 21.8% to 41.2%. **Automated transcript analysis** (UK AISI + Arcadia Impact + Generality Labs, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27518, 2026-07-29) open-sources AI scanners for four validity criteria and finds verified issues in CORE-Bench, CVE-Bench and Terminal-Bench 2.0. **reliability@k** (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14711, 2026-08-11) shows current pass@k implementations substitute test-suite size for rollout count, inflating reported scores by 0.85-0.97 absolute; its SWE-bench pilot recorded macro hidden-test pass rate 0.80 against 1/5 tasks resolved. **Deployment Decision Reliability** (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11323, 2026-08-11) decomposes variance across three open agent-trace benchmarks: the **agent main effect is under 3% of total variance** while agent-by-task interaction is 7-23%, aggregate reliability collapses on the hardest quartile (Erho-squared 0.752 to 0.000), and training-cell reliability correlates *negatively* with held-out reliability (r = -0.90). Leaderboards rank specialisation, not capability.

For open-ended multi-agent settings, **SwarmWorld** (MIT, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.26081, 2026-08-26) is the most honest result of the window: shared physical worlds produce broader and more resilient technological portfolios than a best-of-N isolated-search envelope, but **isolated search can still hold the strongest single artifact**, and explicit communication does not beat physical stigmergy on every endpoint. Their knockout assay is directly reusable: random 50% agent removal leaves 0.983 of artifacts connected, targeted high-degree removal only 0.596.

## 6. Trajectory data pipelines and privacy

**Open-SWE-Traces** (NVIDIA, https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16038, 2026-06-14) releases 207,489 agentic trajectories in nine languages from about 20,000 PRs, filtered to MIT/Apache/BSD repositories, with an AST-based scanner that discards "git hacking" (agents mining reflog/blame for the answer). Two ablations matter for a curator: training on the **full** set including unresolved patches beats resolved-only (58.1 against 55.3 on SWE-V thinking; 47.6 against 40.5 on SWE-M), and cross-harness transfer costs several points in both directions. **SlotGuard** (UIUC, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17147, 2026-07-19) is the redaction design to copy: typed, suffix-aware slots for structural bindings plus format-preserving synthetic substitution for secrets, linked across turns by a session entity graph, with rebinding only inside the trusted runtime. It removes all 20,814 annotated sensitive characters and reduces credential leakage to 0.0% across 852 planted values (typed placeholders alone still leak 23.5%), while keeping task success within 0-10.5 points of raw transcripts where generic redaction collapses to 2.5%; median 14.4 microseconds per turn. **Trajectories That Segment Themselves** (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02302, 2026-08-03) proposes that the acting agent declare its own falsifiable causal hypotheses at collection time so phases become the training unit - small-scale evidence (24/40 boundaries matched against 11.5 random), but it is the cheapest thing to bolt onto an existing session log.

## 7. Governance

**Mapping GPAI governance in twenty AI middle-powers** (Arcadia Impact + The Future Society, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19278, 2026-08-18; dataset on Zenodo, CC-BY-4.0) is the most operationally useful governance paper for a European vendor. Findings that bear on Daliesk: only **22% of mapped GPAI provisions sit in binding law**; ten of twenty jurisdictions hold no binding in-force GPAI provision at all; the EU and Brazil hold more than half of the 85 binding provisions; **outside the EU, no jurisdiction imposes a binding evaluation duty on a model developer**; self-assessment is the majority evaluation model in 11 of 17 jurisdictions; and the compute thresholds do not line up - the EU AI Act presumes systemic risk above **1e25 FLOP** (rebuttable under Art. 52) while Korea's Enforcement Decree sets **1e26** as one of *three cumulative* conditions, so a model trained between them is a systemic-risk GPAI model in the EU and out of scope in Korea. A ~120B open-weight model trained on certified harness runs sits far below both thresholds, which makes the EU's documentation and training-data-summary duties, not the systemic-risk tier, the binding constraint. Two supporting items: an evaluated **12-item agile compliance guideline** validated through 11 expert interviews (https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16526, 2026-08-17), and an empirical study of **about 97.5K AIBOM artifacts** from Hugging Face finding required structural fields complete but model-card, responsible-use, environmental and limitation fields weakly represented or missing (https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17242, 2026-07-19) - the concrete gap a provenance-first release can occupy.

---

## What Daliesk should do

1. **Make `dsh-compaction` a trained seam, not a utility** (goal 3; compaction + session-log seams). CompactionRL's result that swapping only the summariser moves SWE-bench Verified by 6.5 points makes compaction quality a first-order capability lever; adopt its token-level loss normalisation and cross-trajectory GAE correction as the reference design for compacted-rollout training.
2. **Adopt a token-faithful capture boundary before any RL run** (goal 3; `dsh-llm` route + trajectory export). Take LEGO-RL's in-process proxy at the model API and Train-What-You-Deploy's two agent-side commitments: a training mode that provably issues zero background model calls, and per-request provenance headers that **fail closed** rather than guess. The "model-visible implies logged" invariant already supplies most of the accounting; what is missing is capture at the serving boundary and a machine-checked background-call contract.
3. **Gate every environment before it enters training, with execution and not judgement** (goal 4; environment runner + certificates). The 28.5%/25%/16% hackability rates and the 61.9% augmenter defect rate say two things: audit your own registry with a frontier attacker, and never let an LLM judge accept a synthesised check without first running it against the restored fixture. Make gold-sanity execution a hard precondition of certification.
4. **Put a behaviour monitor on the reward, and log its verdict** (goal 3; tamper verdicts + `dsh-guard`). Qwen's monitor took hacked-resolved from 28.57% to 0.56% *and raised* clean resolve by 20 points; the pattern set must be refreshed from the current policy's own rollouts each interval, because hacking is policy-dependent. Plant honeypots as in HVTB so a subset of tamper verdicts is deterministic rather than judged.
5. **Adopt verifier-bounded credit assignment as the default RL rule** (goal 3; training, not agent-loop). CREST's rule - the verifier owns the sign, any teacher only scales the magnitude, gated by entropy - preserves the certified reward as the ceiling, exactly the property a certificates-of-completion pipeline needs. Watch SIGNBALANCE for the guessing failure on bounded-answer environments.
6. **Reconstruct environments from your own certified runs** (goals 3 and 4; trajectory export to environments registry). Terminal-Universe shows a recorded trajectory is a lossy image of its environment: deterministic replay recovered 40.2% sufficiency, agentic completion 93.5%, and re-solving beat imitation by about 15 points. The session log already records every tool call, so the input exists - and held-out environments stay held out because reconstruction never leaves the lab.
7. **Ship redaction as a typed slot boundary, not placeholders** (goal 3; curator with redaction profiles + `dsh-credentials`). SlotGuard's suffix-aware typed slots plus format-preserving synthetic secrets keep task success within a few points of raw transcripts where generic redaction collapses to 2.5%. Redaction profiles should preserve path shape, extension and credential grammar, and be tested with planted secrets and adversarial rebinding cases rather than regex coverage.
8. **Report harness-model pairs with cost, and make the scorekeeper record tokens per certified run** (goals 1 and 4; scorekeeper facts + observatory). Harness choice moves paired pass rate 0-8pp but tokens per solved task up to 41.9x; a leaderboard that omits cost is not a decision instrument. Adopt tokens-per-solved-task, no-action turns and a failure-category vector as first-class scorekeeper facts.
9. **Size experiments with a variance decomposition before trusting a delta** (goal 4; experiments with paired seeds). Agent main effect under 3% of variance, aggregate reliability collapsing to zero on the hardest quartile, and training-cell reliability anti-correlated with held-out reliability (r = -0.90) mean paired seeds alone are insufficient: add a held-out reliability estimate and a difficulty-conditional report per experiment, and compute reliability@k over independent runs rather than tests.
10. **Build the EU AI Act artifacts now, as generated outputs of the composition manifest** (goal 3 and commercial; composition manifest + sign-off records + data-use terms). At about 120B the systemic-risk tier is not the constraint; documentation, the training-data summary and provenance are. Pair the content-addressed component identity already in goal 4 with an AIBOM-shaped release that fills the fields the Hugging Face study found missing - datasets, limitations, responsible use, environmental information - and pin data-use terms to sessions so the training-data summary is a derivation from the ledger rather than a document written afterwards. Use the Zenodo provision dataset to state, per client jurisdiction, which duties actually bind.

1. **LEGO-RL — harness-native RL for coding agents** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17393 (2026-08-18, Huawei + CUHK). Trains inside *unmodified* Claude Code / OpenHands / OpenCode via an in-process proxy that captures exact token ids, masks and MoE routing. Qwen3.5-35B-A3B: SWE-bench Verified 64.0→70.4 / 62.4→68.2 / 57.2→66.6, rollout-training correlation >0.99. This is goal 3's architecture, published.
2. **Terminal-Universe — trajectories reconstructed into environments** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04148 (2026-09-03, Qwen Team). 359,593 trajectories → 37,273 task-sufficient environments; replay alone gives 40.2% sufficiency, agentic completion 93.5%; SFT gives +11.9 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. Daliesk's session log is already the required input, and reconstruction never exports anything.
3. **Auditing Reward Hackability in Code RL Environments** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16062 (2026-06-14). 28.5% of SWE-bench Verified and 25.0% of R2E-Gym accept a verified-incorrect patch; +14.14pp Pass@1 inflation on hackable tasks across 134 frontier submissions; and a **61.9% defect rate in LLM-authored hardening tests** that an LLM judge missed but a gold-sanity execution gate caught.
4. **DarwinX — evolving harnesses under a preserve-and-extend contract** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07545 (2026-07-31, Salesforce). Model frozen: Terminal-Bench 2.1 75.5→83.2% (84.7% on a stronger base), WebArena-Infinity audit-clean 43.5→93.0%, harness transfers unchanged to SWE-bench Verified at 84.2%. The bounded-regression promotion rule is directly reusable as goal 4's sign-off gate — and doubles as a compliance interface.
5. **Mapping GPAI governance in twenty AI middle-powers** — https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19278 (2026-08-18, Arcadia Impact + The Future Society). Only 22% of GPAI provisions are binding; outside the EU no jurisdiction imposes a binding evaluation duty on a model developer; EU 10²⁵ FLOP (rebuttable) vs Korea 10²⁶ as one of three cumulative conditions. At ~120B the binding constraints are documentation, transparency and the training-data summary, not the systemic-risk tier.

**Cross-cutting findings worth flagging to the other two researchers:** the harness became a *measured* object this quarter (HarnessOpt-Bench, HarnessDev, EvoHarnessBench in five weeks); harness choice moves pass rate 0–8pp but tokens-per-solved-task up to **41.9×** (Scaffold Effect); skill-loading comparisons are invalid without caching-correct accounting since cache reads are **74–94%** of multi-turn input (Skill Blocks); and the agent main effect is **under 3% of variance** on three open agent-trace benchmarks, with training-cell reliability *anti*-correlated with held-out reliability at r = −0.90 (Deployment Decision Reliability) — so paired seeds alone do not license a claimed delta.
